label: Estimating a 2D Homography
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 87 through 131, asks one question: given noisy point matches between two images of a plane, recover the homography that relates them. We preview the route from the linear DLT solver, through normalization and geometric cost, to maximum-likelihood refinement and robust RANSAC estimation.

label: The Estimation Problem
notes: A planar projective map is a three by three matrix acting on homogeneous coordinates. It has nine entries but only eight degrees of freedom because overall scale is irrelevant. Four general correspondences fix it exactly; with more, noisy matches, we must minimise some cost and choose which one carefully.

label: DLT: Cross-Product Constraint
notes: Each correspondence forces the image point and the mapped point to be parallel as homogeneous vectors, so their cross product vanishes. Expanding that cross product gives three scalar equations linear in the entries of H, of which only two are independent. This is the algebraic heart of the Direct Linear Transformation.

label: Stacking Rows and SVD
notes: Two independent rows per match stack into a design matrix A, and we seek the vector h with A h equal to zero. With exact data the matrix has rank eight and a one-dimensional nullspace. The singular value decomposition returns that null vector as the right singular vector of smallest singular value.

label: Data Normalization
notes: Raw pixel DLT mixes entries near one with products near a million, wrecking conditioning. Hartley normalization translates each point cloud to its centroid and scales it so the mean distance from the origin equals root two. This similarity changes coordinates, not geometry, yet dramatically improves the numerical nullspace problem.

label: Algebraic vs Geometric Error
notes: DLT minimises the algebraic residual, the norm of A h, whose units are not pixels. The geometric error instead measures reprojection distance in the image plane, where the points actually live. The two disagree, and a small algebraic residual is no guarantee of small pixel error before normalization.

label: Reprojection and Sampson Error
notes: Symmetric transfer error sums squared distances in both images. The reprojection error also estimates corrected points lying exactly on the map. The Sampson error is a first-order approximation of that geometric cost, cheap to compute yet far closer to the true geometric distance than the raw algebraic residual.

label: Maximum Likelihood Estimate
notes: Under independent isotropic Gaussian measurement noise, the negative log likelihood is exactly the sum of squared geometric reprojection errors. So minimising geometric error is the maximum-likelihood estimate. The gold-standard algorithm initialises with normalized DLT, then iteratively refines using Levenberg-Marquardt over the homography and corrected points.

label: Robust Estimation: RANSAC
notes: Real correspondences contain mismatches that no least-squares cost can survive. RANSAC repeatedly draws a minimal sample of four matches, fits a homography, and counts inliers agreeing within a pixel threshold. The model with the largest support wins, and the homography is then refined on its inlier set.

label: Choosing the RANSAC Threshold
notes: The inlier threshold must match the expected localization noise. Set it too small and good matches are rejected; too large and outliers are admitted. The required sample count grows with the outlier fraction, so the probability of drawing one all-inlier minimal set drives the adaptive iteration budget.

label: Degenerate Configurations
notes: Four points define a homography only if no three are collinear; nearly collinear or tightly clustered points give an ill-conditioned design even when algebraically solvable. RANSAC samples can also be degenerate, fitting a spurious map. Detecting and rejecting these configurations protects both the linear solver and the robust estimator.

label: The Estimation Workflow
notes: Putting it together: normalized DLT gives a conditioned linear initialization, RANSAC isolates a coherent inlier set when matches are contaminated, and maximum-likelihood refinement minimises pixel reprojection error from that start. Always compare homographies by their action on points, never by raw matrix entries, since the map is scale-free.
